blueprint.coverage_deficit_addressed: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension — Idiopathic intracranial hypertension is a syndrome of increased intracranial pressure without an intracranial mass, hydrocephalus, venous sinus thrombosis, or other identified structural cause. It commonly presents with headache, papilledema, transient visual symptoms, pulsatile tinnitus, and sometimes sixth-nerve palsy. Diagnosis requires exclusion of secondary causes with neuroimaging and demonstration of elevated cerebrospinal-fluid opening pressure with otherwise normal CSF composition.

distractor_explanations.A: Incorrect. Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis can produce headache, papilledema, visual symptoms, and elevated intracranial pressure. However, MR venography is specifically used to detect venous sinus thrombosis, and the normal MR venogram in this vignette argues against that secondary cause.
distractor_explanations.B: Incorrect. Migraine with aura can cause headache and transient visual phenomena, but it does not explain bilateral papilledema and objectively elevated CSF opening pressure.
distractor_explanations.C: Incorrect. Optic neuritis typically causes acute loss of vision in one eye, impaired color vision, and pain with eye movement. It does not cause a syndrome of generalized intracranial hypertension with bilateral papilledema and pulsatile tinnitus.
distractor_explanations.D: Incorrect. Normal-pressure hydrocephalus classically causes a gait disorder, cognitive impairment, and urinary symptoms with ventricular enlargement. This patient instead has papilledema, pulsatile tinnitus, elevated opening pressure, and no hydrocephalus on imaging.
distractor_explanations.E: Correct. This patient has idiopathic intracranial hypertension. MedlinePlus describes IIH as increased intracranial pressure without an identified intracranial mass and lists headache, visual symptoms, pulsatile tinnitus, papilledema, and possible sixth-nerve palsy among its manifestations. The diagnosis is supported here by bilateral papilledema, transient visual obscurations, pulse-synchronous tinnitus, a normal MRI/MR venogram excluding mass and venous thrombosis, normal CSF composition, and an elevated opening pressure.

item.vignette: A 29-year-old woman has 6 weeks of progressively frequent headaches, brief episodes of dimming vision when she bends over, and a rhythmic whooshing sound in both ears that matches her pulse. BMI is 36 kg/m². Funduscopic examination shows bilateral optic-disc swelling. Neurologic examination is otherwise normal. MRI of the brain and MR venography show no mass, hydrocephalus, or venous sinus thrombosis. Lumbar puncture shows markedly elevated opening pressure with normal cerebrospinal-fluid composition.

blueprint.coverage_deficit_addressed: Exogenous insulin administration — Endogenous pancreatic beta cells synthesize proinsulin and cleave it into insulin and C-peptide before secretion. Exogenous insulin provides insulin without accompanying C-peptide or proinsulin. Therefore, during hypoglycemia caused by exogenous insulin, circulating insulin is inappropriately elevated while endogenous C-peptide and proinsulin are suppressed. Insulin secretagogues and insulinoma instead stimulate endogenous insulin secretion and therefore raise C-peptide; a secretagogue screen helps distinguish medication ingestion from insulinoma.
official_outline_path: Hypoglycemia secondary to surreptitious insulin use
blueprint.primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination

distractor_explanations.A: Incorrect. Insulinoma causes endogenous hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia. Because insulin and C-peptide are co-secreted by pancreatic beta cells, insulinoma is associated with inappropriately elevated insulin together with elevated C-peptide and proinsulin during hypoglycemia, not suppression of C-peptide and proinsulin.
distractor_explanations.B: Incorrect. Sulfonylureas and other insulin secretagogues stimulate pancreatic insulin release, producing elevated insulin together with elevated C-peptide. Detection of the drug in blood or urine distinguishes secretagogue exposure from insulinoma; this patient's secretagogue screen is negative and C-peptide is suppressed.
distractor_explanations.C: Correct. This biochemical pattern indicates exogenous insulin exposure. Insulin and C-peptide are produced together when endogenous pancreatic beta cells secrete insulin. In contrast, injected insulin contains no C-peptide; therefore, exogenous insulin–induced hypoglycemia produces inappropriately high insulin with suppressed C-peptide and proinsulin. Insulinoma and sulfonylurea exposure both stimulate endogenous insulin secretion and therefore do not fit the suppressed C-peptide pattern; a negative secretagogue screen additionally argues against sulfonylurea or meglitinide ingestion.
distractor_explanations.D: Incorrect. Some non-islet-cell tumors cause hypoglycemia through excess IGF-2 signaling. Endotext notes that insulin and C-peptide are appropriately suppressed during this form of hypoglycemia, so it does not match the inappropriately elevated insulin level in this patient.
distractor_explanations.E: Incorrect. Cortisol deficiency can impair the counterregulatory response to hypoglycemia, but primary adrenal insufficiency does not produce the distinctive combination of elevated insulin with suppressed C-peptide and proinsulin. Typical associated findings can include hyperpigmentation and electrolyte abnormalities, which are absent here.

item.vignette: A 32-year-old woman without diabetes is evaluated for recurrent episodes of diaphoresis, tremor, confusion, and near-syncope that improve promptly after she consumes glucose. During a supervised symptomatic episode, plasma glucose is low. At the same time, plasma insulin is inappropriately elevated, whereas C-peptide and proinsulin are suppressed. A serum screen for sulfonylureas and meglitinides is negative. Liver and kidney function are normal, and she has no hyperpigmentation or electrolyte abnormalities.

blueprint.coverage_deficit_addressed: Pacemaker failure to capture — Failure to capture occurs when a pacemaker delivers an electrical pacing impulse but the myocardium does not depolarize in response. On the surface ECG, a pacing spike is present without a subsequent evoked P wave or QRS complex. This differs from output failure, in which the expected pacing spike is absent; undersensing, in which intrinsic depolarizations are not detected and pacing occurs inappropriately; and oversensing, in which non-target electrical signals inappropriately inhibit pacing.

distractor_explanations.A: Incorrect. Output failure is failure of the pacemaker to generate an impulse and is characterized by absence of the expected pacing spike. This patient has clearly visible pacing spikes, including spikes that fail to evoke ventricular depolarization.
distractor_explanations.B: Correct. This is ventricular failure to capture. The pacemaker is generating ventricular pacing impulses, visible as pacing spikes, but some spikes are not followed by ventricular depolarization. The preserved output and intact sensing in this vignette specifically distinguish capture failure from output and sensing abnormalities.
distractor_explanations.C: Incorrect. Undersensing occurs when the device fails to detect intrinsic cardiac activity, causing pacing spikes to appear despite spontaneous P waves or QRS complexes. distractor_explanations.D: Incorrect. Oversensing occurs when the pacemaker detects inappropriate electrical signals and inhibits pacing when a stimulus is needed. That produces fewer or absent pacing spikes during inappropriate inhibition, rather than visible spikes that fail to depolarize the ventricle.
distractor_explanations.E: Incorrect. Pacemaker-mediated tachycardia is a reentrant tachyarrhythmia involving a dual-chamber pacemaker and produces inappropriate rapid paced ventricular activity. This patient instead has pauses because some delivered ventricular impulses do not evoke a QRS complex.

item.vignette: A 76-year-old man with complete atrioventricular block and a permanent dual-chamber pacemaker presents with intermittent lightheadedness. Blood pressure is 108/64 mm Hg. blueprint.coverage_deficit_addressed: Assess willingness to quit within the 5 A's tobacco-cessation framework — The 5 A's framework organizes tobacco-cessation counseling as Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, and Arrange. After tobacco use has been identified and the clinician has clearly advised cessation, the next step is to assess whether the patient is willing to make a quit attempt at this time. Assistance with a quit plan or pharmacotherapy follows for a patient who is willing, and follow-up is then arranged.

distractor_explanations.A: Incorrect. Medication selection and development of a quit plan are part of the Assist step. In the 5 A's sequence, the clinician first assesses willingness to make a quit attempt after asking about tobacco use and advising cessation.
distractor_explanations.B: Correct. The physician has already completed Ask by identifying tobacco use and Advise by clearly recommending cessation. The next 5 A's step is Assess: determine whether the patient is willing to make a quit attempt now. AHRQ lists the sequence as Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, and Arrange and specifically defines Assess as asking whether the tobacco user is willing to make a quit attempt at this time. Assistance and follow-up depend on that response.
distractor_explanations.C: Incorrect. Arrange is the follow-up step and comes after assessment and appropriate assistance. The immediate next task is to determine readiness to make a quit attempt.
distractor_explanations.D: Incorrect. The Ask step has already been completed because the physician has identified and documented current tobacco use.
distractor_explanations.E: Incorrect. Exploring barriers and other motivational strategies can be appropriate for a patient who is not ready to quit, but willingness should first be assessed explicitly.

blueprint.coverage_deficit_addressed: Nonrandom shift on a run chart — A run chart displays a measure in time order around a median. Run-chart rules are used to distinguish likely nonrandom change from ordinary variation. For a run chart with fewer than 20 data points, six or more consecutive points entirely above or below the median constitute a shift; points on the median are not counted. A shift is a signal that the underlying process may have changed and should be investigated in relation to interventions or other events.
official_outline_path: Measurement tools: run and control charts
blueprint.primary_competency: Practice-Based Learning and Improvement
blueprint.primary_system: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills

distractor_explanations.A: Correct. This is a run-chart shift. IHI's run-chart rules define a shift as six or more consecutive points above or below the median when the chart contains fewer than 20 total data points, excluding points on the median. This chart has 16 points and six consecutive post-intervention observations below the baseline median, so it signals nonrandom change. Because the values are not steadily decreasing, the pattern is not a trend. The signal supports further interpretation of the process change but does not by itself prove causality.
distractor_explanations.B: Incorrect. Run charts do not require control limits to identify nonrandom patterns. Control limits are a feature of control charts; run-chart rules use the median and the pattern of points over time.
distractor_explanations.C: Incorrect. A trend requires sequential points that continually increase or decrease. These six values fluctuate but remain on one side of the median, which is a shift rather than a trend.
distractor_explanations.D: Incorrect. A run-chart shift is evidence of a nonrandom change in the process, but temporal association alone does not prove that the intervention caused the change; other contemporaneous factors should still be considered.
distractor_explanations.E: Incorrect. Quality-improvement run charts are specifically designed to detect nonrandom patterns over time using run-chart rules. A conventional p-value hypothesis test is not required before recognizing a shift signal.

blueprint.coverage_deficit_addressed: Brucellosis — Brucellosis is a systemic zoonotic bacterial infection acquired through contact with infected animals or consumption of contaminated animal products, especially unpasteurized milk or cheese. Clinical illness is nonspecific but commonly includes fever, sweats, fatigue, myalgia, arthralgia, weight loss, and focal organ involvement; osteoarticular symptoms and hepatosplenomegaly can occur. Exposure history is therefore central to recognizing the diagnosis, which requires laboratory confirmation.

blueprint.coverage_deficit_addressed: Retinitis pigmentosa with preferential early rod photoreceptor degeneration — Retinitis pigmentosa is a genetically heterogeneous group of inherited retinal dystrophies. In the typical rod-cone form, rod photoreceptors are preferentially affected early. Progressive rod dysfunction causes nyctalopia and peripheral visual-field loss; cone dysfunction develops later and can impair color and central vision. Retinal pigment epithelium becomes secondarily abnormal, and migrating pigment-containing cells contribute to the characteristic bone-spicule fundus appearance.
blueprint.primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
blueprint.primary_system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses

distractor_explanations.A: Incorrect. Cone dysfunction can occur later in retinitis pigmentosa and contributes to impaired color discrimination and central visual loss. The early combination of nyctalopia and peripheral-field constriction reflects preferential rod dysfunction.
distractor_explanations.B: Incorrect. Retinal pigment epithelium becomes abnormal as photoreceptor degeneration progresses, and pigment migration contributes to bone-spicule deposits. In the typical rod-cone form, the primary early photoreceptor loss is rod-predominant.
distractor_explanations.C: Incorrect. Retinal ganglion cells are output neurons whose axons form the optic nerve; they are not the preferentially affected early photoreceptor population in typical retinitis pigmentosa.
distractor_explanations.D: Incorrect. Bipolar cells relay signals from photoreceptors to inner retinal neurons. The characteristic early defect in typical retinitis pigmentosa is degeneration of rods rather than preferential primary bipolar-cell loss.
distractor_explanations.E: Correct. This patient has classic retinitis pigmentosa: progressive night blindness followed by peripheral visual-field constriction with bone-spicule retinal pigmentation. In the typical rod-cone form, genetic defects preferentially impair rod photoreceptors early. Because rods mediate scotopic vision and are concentrated outside the fovea, rod loss produces nyctalopia and progressive peripheral-field loss before central cone-mediated vision is substantially affected. Cone and retinal pigment epithelial abnormalities become more prominent later.

Progressive rod dysfunction causes nyctalopia and peripheral visual-field loss; cone dysfunction develops later and can impair color and central vision. Retinal pigment epithelium becomes secondarily abnormal, and migrating pigment-containing cells contribute to the characteristic bone-spicule fundus appearance.

distractor_explanations.A: Correct. Octreotide exerts actions similar to somatostatin and suppresses growth hormone secretion. Somatostatin receptors are GPCRs coupled to inhibitory G proteins. Activation of Gi inhibits adenylyl cyclase, lowering intracellular cAMP; somatostatin-receptor activation also lowers intracellular calcium, reinforcing inhibition of secretory activity. The other options represent distinct receptor-signaling families rather than the somatostatin-receptor pathway.
distractor_explanations.B: Incorrect. Gs-coupled receptors stimulate adenylyl cyclase and increase cAMP. Somatostatin receptors instead exert inhibitory signaling that includes Gi-mediated suppression of adenylyl cyclase.
distractor_explanations.C: Incorrect. Gq-coupled receptors activate phospholipase C, generating IP3 and diacylglycerol and increasing intracellular calcium. This is not the characteristic inhibitory G-protein pathway of somatostatin receptors.
distractor_explanations.D: Incorrect. Intrinsic receptor tyrosine kinases autophosphorylate after ligand binding and can activate pathways such as PI3K-Akt; the insulin receptor is a classic endocrine example. Somatostatin receptors are GPCRs rather than intrinsic receptor tyrosine kinases.
distractor_explanations.E: Incorrect. Some cytokine-family hormone receptors signal through receptor-associated JAK kinases and STAT proteins. Somatostatin receptors instead are inhibitory GPCRs.

blueprint.coverage_deficit_addressed: Abetalipoproteinemia due to MTTP deficiency — Microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTTP/MTP) transfers triglyceride and other neutral lipids to nascent apolipoprotein B within the endoplasmic reticulum. This step is required for assembly and secretion of apoB-containing lipoproteins: chylomicrons from intestinal epithelial cells and VLDL from hepatocytes. Biallelic loss-of-function MTTP variants cause abetalipoproteinemia, with extremely low or absent apoB-containing lipoproteins, fat and fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption, acanthocytosis, and progressive neurologic/retinal complications if untreated.
official_outline_path: Disorders of the stomach, small intestine, colon, rectum, anus
blueprint.primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts

distractor_explanations.A: Incorrect. Lipoprotein lipase acts extracellularly on circulating triglyceride-rich lipoproteins. Deficiency causes marked hypertriglyceridemia and chylomicronemia rather than nearly absent apoB-containing lipoproteins.
distractor_explanations.B: Incorrect. SAR1B defects cause chylomicron retention disease by impairing prechylomicron transport from ER to Golgi. They primarily disrupt intestinal chylomicron secretion rather than the global MTTP-dependent assembly of both intestinal chylomicrons and hepatic VLDL.
distractor_explanations.C: Incorrect. LCAT esterifies cholesterol in plasma, especially during HDL maturation. LCAT deficiency does not prevent apoB-containing lipoprotein assembly in the ER.
distractor_explanations.D: Correct. The findings indicate abetalipoproteinemia caused by MTTP deficiency. MTTP is located in the endoplasmic reticulum of enterocytes and hepatocytes and transfers neutral lipid to nascent apoB. Without this lipid-transfer step, apoB-containing lipoproteins cannot be assembled and secreted normally, producing a severe deficiency of chylomicrons, VLDL, and LDL. The resulting fat and fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption explains the low vitamin E, neurologic findings, and acanthocytosis.
distractor_explanations.E: Incorrect. LDL-receptor deficiency impairs LDL clearance and causes high LDL cholesterol rather than extremely low LDL and apoB.

explanation.educational_objective: Connect abetalipoproteinemia to loss of MTTP-mediated lipid transfer onto nascent apoB in the endoplasmic reticulum, preventing formation of chylomicrons and VLDL and causing fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption.
explanation.key_explanation: The findings indicate abetalipoproteinemia caused by MTTP deficiency. MTTP is located in the endoplasmic reticulum of enterocytes and hepatocytes and transfers neutral lipid to nascent apoB. Without this lipid-transfer step, apoB-containing lipoproteins cannot be assembled and secreted normally, producing a severe deficiency of chylomicrons, VLDL, and LDL. The resulting fat and fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption explains the low vitamin E, neurologic findings, and acanthocytosis.

item.tested_construct: Microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTTP/MTP) transfers triglyceride and other neutral lipids to nascent apolipoprotein B within the endoplasmic reticulum. This step is required for assembly and secretion of apoB-containing lipoproteins: chylomicrons from intestinal epithelial cells and VLDL from hepatocytes. Biallelic loss-of-function MTTP variants cause abetalipoproteinemia, with extremely low or absent apoB-containing lipoproteins, fat and fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption, acanthocytosis, and progressive neurologic/retinal complications if untreated.
item.vignette: An 8-year-old boy has chronic bulky greasy stools, poor weight gain, and progressive unsteadiness while walking. Examination shows diminished ankle reflexes. Peripheral blood smear shows numerous acanthocytes. Serum vitamin E is markedly reduced, and plasma apolipoprotein B is nearly undetectable. His LDL cholesterol and triglyceride concentrations are extremely low.

distractor_explanations.A: Incorrect. Calciphylaxis is strongly associated with end-stage renal disease, but it classically causes extremely painful ischemic skin lesions that may become violaceous, ulcerated, necrotic, or covered by eschar rather than symmetric woody fibrotic plaques with contractures after gadolinium exposure.
distractor_explanations.B: Incorrect. Diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis can cause widespread skin thickening and contractures, but the combination of advanced kidney failure, recent gadolinium-based contrast exposure, symmetric woody plaques beginning distally, and facial sparing is much more characteristic of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis.
distractor_explanations.C: Correct. This patient has nephrogenic systemic fibrosis. The decisive pattern is advanced kidney failure with recent gadolinium-based contrast exposure followed by symmetric, hard or woody induration of the extremities, progressive proximal spread, and flexion contractures with relative sparing of the face. Current gadolinium-based contrast labeling warns that nephrogenic systemic fibrosis occurs in patients with impaired elimination of these agents and may cause debilitating fibrosis of skin, muscle, and internal organs.
distractor_explanations.D: Incorrect. Eosinophilic fasciitis can produce symmetric woody induration of the extremities and contractures, making it a plausible mimic, but it is not specifically linked to gadolinium exposure in advanced kidney failure and usually reflects eosinophilic inflammation of deep fascia.
distractor_explanations.E: Incorrect. Scleromyxedema is a scleroderma-like disorder typically associated with waxy papules and monoclonal gammopathy and commonly involves the face or neck, unlike the classic facial sparing of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis.

distractor_explanations.C: Incorrect. distractor_explanations.D: Correct. This patient has cat-scratch disease caused by Bartonella henselae. distractor_explanations.E: Incorrect. item.vignette: A 12-year-old girl is brought to the clinic because of a painful swelling in her right axilla and low-grade fever. Three weeks ago, her family adopted a kitten. While she was playing with it, one of its claws broke the skin on the dorsum of her right hand. The kitten remains well and has no visible skin lesions. A small papule developed at the injury site and is still visible. Examination shows a tender 3-cm right axillary lymph node. There is no pharyngitis, cervical lymphadenopathy, or hepatosplenomegaly.

blueprint.coverage_deficit_addressed: Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), classic Richardson syndrome phenotype — Progressive supranuclear palsy is an atypical parkinsonian neurodegenerative tauopathy. Pathology includes predominantly 4-repeat tau accumulation in neurons and glia with degeneration involving basal ganglia and brainstem/oculomotor structures. The classic clinical phenotype combines early postural instability with backward falls, axial-predominant rigidity, and supranuclear impairment of vertical eye movements.
blueprint.primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
blueprint.primary_system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses

distractor_explanations.A: Correct. This patient has progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP). The most discriminating combination is early unexplained backward falls, axial-predominant rigidity with an extended posture, minimal response to levodopa, and marked slowing/limitation of vertical eye movements, especially downward gaze. PSP is an atypical parkinsonian syndrome associated with tau pathology and is explicitly included in the 2026 USMLE Nervous System content outline.
distractor_explanations.B: Incorrect. Idiopathic Parkinson disease can cause bradykinesia and rigidity, but early backward falls, axial-predominant extended posture, prominent vertical gaze impairment, and little levodopa benefit favor progressive supranuclear palsy. Parkinson disease more often has a flexed posture and a stronger levodopa response.
distractor_explanations.C: Incorrect. Multiple system atrophy is another atypical parkinsonian disorder and may respond poorly to levodopa, but prominent autonomic dysfunction and/or cerebellar features are characteristic. Vertical supranuclear gaze palsy with early backward falls and axial rigidity is more characteristic of progressive supranuclear palsy.
distractor_explanations.D: Incorrect. Corticobasal syndrome can cause parkinsonism, but it classically has an asymmetric limb-predominant presentation with cortical features such as apraxia, cortical sensory loss, myoclonus, dystonia, or an alien-limb phenomenon. The symmetric axial pattern with vertical gaze impairment favors progressive supranuclear palsy.
distractor_explanations.E: Incorrect. Dementia with Lewy bodies can produce parkinsonism, but early cognitive decline with fluctuations, recurrent visual hallucinations, and REM sleep behavior disorder are characteristic clues. The dominant pattern here is early postural instability plus axial rigidity and vertical supranuclear gaze dysfunction.

item.vignette: A 68-year-old man is evaluated for 2 years of progressive gait difficulty and slowed movement. During the first year of illness, he began falling unexpectedly, usually backward. A trial of carbidopa/levodopa produced little improvement. Examination shows bradykinesia and marked rigidity of the neck and trunk with a relatively extended posture. Resting tremor is minimal. When he follows the examiner's finger, vertical saccades are markedly slowed and downward gaze is limited; horizontal eye movements are much less affected.

before_BATCH_CLINICAL_Q0659_Q0683_202609.claim: Progressive supranuclear palsy is the uniquely best answer. This patient has progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP). The most discriminating combination is early unexplained backward falls, axial-predominant rigidity with an extended posture, minimal response to levodopa, and marked slowing/limitation of vertical eye movements, especially downward gaze. PSP is an atypical parkinsonian syndrome associated with tau pathology and is explicitly included in the 2026 USMLE Nervous System content outline.

before_BATCH_CLINICAL_Q0659_Q0683_202609.claim: Idiopathic Parkinson disease is incorrect for this vignette. Idiopathic Parkinson disease can cause bradykinesia and rigidity, but early backward falls, axial-predominant extended posture, prominent vertical gaze impairment, and little levodopa benefit favor progressive supranuclear palsy. Parkinson disease more often has a flexed posture and a stronger levodopa response.

blueprint.coverage_deficit_addressed: Anomalous left coronary artery from the pulmonary artery (ALCAPA) — In ALCAPA, the left coronary artery originates from the pulmonary artery rather than the aorta. Early after birth, relatively high pulmonary artery pressure can maintain some antegrade perfusion through the anomalous vessel. As pulmonary vascular resistance and pulmonary artery pressure fall, left-coronary perfusion pressure decreases and flow can reverse toward the low-pressure pulmonary artery; collateral flow from the right coronary system is then partly lost into the pulmonary artery (coronary steal), producing left-ventricular myocardial ischemia.
official_outline_path: Congenital disorders, including disease in adults
blueprint.primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts

distractor_explanations.A: Correct. The infant has ALCAPA. Soon after birth, pulmonary artery pressure remains relatively high, so the anomalous left coronary artery can still receive some antegrade flow. As pulmonary vascular resistance and pulmonary artery pressure fall, left-coronary perfusion pressure falls and antegrade flow diminishes. Blood supplied through right-to-left coronary collaterals can then run retrograde through the anomalous left coronary artery into the lower-pressure pulmonary artery, creating coronary steal and causing left-ventricular ischemia, dysfunction, and secondary mitral regurgitation.
distractor_explanations.B: Incorrect. Acute-angle ostial narrowing and an intramural/interarterial course can make a coronary artery arising from the opposite aortic sinus hemodynamically significant. This infant's left coronary artery instead originates from the pulmonary artery; the relevant postnatal mechanism is falling pulmonary arterial pressure with loss and reversal of left-coronary perfusion, not an aortic intramural course.
distractor_explanations.C: Incorrect. An intramyocardial coronary course (myocardial bridge) can rarely cause ischemia through systolic vessel compression. No intramyocardial course is described here, and that mechanism does not explain why ALCAPA becomes symptomatic as pulmonary vascular resistance and pulmonary artery pressure fall after birth.
distractor_explanations.D: Incorrect. A coronary artery fistula can cause steal by maintaining antegrade flow that bypasses the myocardial capillary bed into a low-resistance chamber or vessel. ALCAPA is mechanistically different: the anomalous left coronary originates from the pulmonary artery, and after pulmonary pressure falls, flow tends to reverse from the higher-pressure coronary collateral network into the lower-pressure pulmonary artery.
distractor_explanations.E: Incorrect. Systemic vascular resistance does rise after placental separation and can increase left ventricular afterload, making this a plausible supply-demand alternative. However, ALCAPA does not preserve stable antegrade pulmonary-artery-to-left-coronary perfusion; the critical change is the fall in pulmonary pressure/resistance, which reduces antegrade flow and promotes retrograde coronary steal.

explanation.educational_objective: Explain why infants with ALCAPA often become symptomatic after an initially well neonatal period: falling pulmonary vascular resistance and pulmonary artery pressure reduce antegrade left-coronary perfusion and promote retrograde coronary steal into the pulmonary artery.

item.difficulty_basis: Moderate-hard author estimate: requires applying postnatal pressure changes to anomalous coronary flow and steal physiology.
item.lead_in: Which of the following mechanisms most directly explains the onset of this infant's myocardial ischemia during the transition to postnatal circulation?

options.A: A fall in pulmonary vascular resistance lowers pulmonary artery pressure, promoting reduced antegrade and then retrograde flow through the anomalous left coronary artery into the pulmonary artery
options.B: Rising aortic pressure produces flow limitation in an acute-angle intramural left coronary artery arising from the opposite aortic sinus
options.C: Feeding-related tachycardia produces ischemia by systolic compression of an intramyocardial left coronary segment
options.D: Antegrade flow through a coronary-to-pulmonary arterial fistula bypasses the myocardial capillary bed and produces a steal phenomenon
options.E: The postnatal rise in systemic vascular resistance raises left ventricular oxygen demand while antegrade pulmonary-artery-to-left-coronary flow remains preserved

item.vignette: A 6-week-old infant is evaluated for recurrent episodes of intense crying, pallor, diaphoresis, and tachypnea during feeding. The infant was well during the first days after birth. Echocardiography shows left ventricular systolic dysfunction and mitral regurgitation. The left coronary artery arises from the main pulmonary artery rather than the aortic root.

blueprint.coverage_deficit_addressed: Pulmonary arteriovenous malformation (pulmonary arteriovenous fistula) producing an anatomic intrapulmonary right-to-left shunt — A pulmonary arteriovenous malformation directly connects a branch of the pulmonary arterial circulation with the pulmonary venous circulation, allowing a fraction of deoxygenated venous blood to bypass ventilated alveoli and the pulmonary capillary gas-exchange interface. This anatomic right-to-left shunt raises the alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient and produces hypoxemia that improves poorly even when inspired oxygen concentration is markedly increased because the shunted blood never contacts alveolar gas.

distractor_explanations.A: Incorrect. Low V/Q regions can cause hypoxemia and an increased A-a gradient, but increasing inspired oxygen generally improves oxygenation because blood still passes capillaries adjacent to ventilated alveoli. In an anatomic right-to-left shunt, some blood never contacts alveolar gas, making the hypoxemia substantially less responsive to oxygen.
distractor_explanations.B: Correct. The vascular connection is a pulmonary arteriovenous malformation (pulmonary arteriovenous fistula). It creates an anatomic intrapulmonary right-to-left shunt: deoxygenated pulmonary arterial blood reaches the pulmonary venous circulation without traversing alveolar capillaries. Raising inspired oxygen markedly increases alveolar oxygen tension in ventilated units, but it cannot oxygenate the fraction of blood that bypasses those units. The resulting admixture therefore produces an increased A-a gradient with hypoxemia that is notably resistant to correction with supplemental oxygen.
distractor_explanations.C: Incorrect. Diffusion limitation can increase the A-a gradient when oxygen transfer across an abnormal alveolar-capillary membrane is impaired, but the presented structural lesion is a direct artery-to-vein channel that bypasses the membrane entirely. Supplemental oxygen can increase the diffusion driving pressure in diffusion-limited disease.
distractor_explanations.D: Incorrect. Pure alveolar hypoventilation lowers alveolar and arterial oxygen tension together and characteristically has a normal A-a gradient. This patient has an increased A-a gradient and an anatomic vessel that bypasses alveolar gas exchange.
distractor_explanations.E: Incorrect. High V/Q or dead-space physiology occurs when ventilation is present but perfusion is deficient. A pulmonary arteriovenous malformation does the opposite with respect to oxygenation: blood is perfused through a vascular shortcut that bypasses ventilated alveoli and the capillary gas-exchange surface.

item.difficulty_basis: Moderate author estimate: requires distinguishing an anatomic shunt from low V/Q, diffusion limitation, and hypoventilation.
item.lead_in: Which of the following mechanisms best explains this patient's persistent hypoxemia despite the marked increase in inspired oxygen concentration?

options.A: Blood traverses alveoli with reduced ventilation relative to perfusion, producing a low ventilation-perfusion ratio
options.B: A portion of venous blood bypasses ventilated alveoli through a direct pulmonary artery-to-vein connection and then mixes with oxygenated pulmonary venous blood
options.C: Oxygen equilibration is slowed by increased thickness of the alveolar-capillary diffusion barrier
options.D: Global alveolar ventilation is reduced, lowering alveolar oxygen tension without increasing the alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient
options.E: Ventilated alveoli receive little or no perfusion, increasing physiologic dead space

item.tested_construct: A pulmonary arteriovenous malformation directly connects a branch of the pulmonary arterial circulation with the pulmonary venous circulation, allowing a fraction of deoxygenated venous blood to bypass ventilated alveoli and the pulmonary capillary gas-exchange interface. This anatomic right-to-left shunt raises the alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient and produces hypoxemia that improves poorly even when inspired oxygen concentration is markedly increased because the shunted blood never contacts alveolar gas.
item.vignette: A 29-year-old woman with recurrent spontaneous epistaxis and small telangiectasias on the lips and fingertips is evaluated for exertional dyspnea and cyanosis. Contrast-enhanced chest imaging shows a direct vascular communication between a branch of the pulmonary artery and a pulmonary vein. Arterial blood gas analysis shows hypoxemia with an increased alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient. Her arterial oxygen tension rises only modestly while she breathes 100% oxygen.

blueprint.coverage_deficit_addressed: Familial glucocorticoid deficiency type 1 due to MC2R loss-of-function (ACTH resistance) — MC2R is the adrenal ACTH receptor and signals predominantly through Gs to adenylyl cyclase, cAMP, and protein kinase A in zona fasciculata cells to promote cortisol steroidogenesis. Loss of MC2R function therefore produces ACTH resistance with low cortisol and compensatory high ACTH. Mineralocorticoid secretion is classically preserved because aldosterone production in the zona glomerulosa is regulated primarily by angiotensin II and extracellular potassium through calcium-dependent signaling rather than by ACTH.
blueprint.primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts

distractor_explanations.A: Incorrect. Impaired angiotensin II signaling in zona glomerulosa would reduce aldosterone secretion and tend to increase renin and disturb sodium/potassium homeostasis. This patient instead has normal renin and aldosterone with isolated glucocorticoid deficiency.
distractor_explanations.B: Incorrect. Severe StAR dysfunction impairs the delivery of cholesterol to the inner mitochondrial membrane, compromising synthesis of multiple adrenal steroid classes rather than selectively disrupting ACTH responsiveness. It would not explain classically preserved mineralocorticoid secretion in an MC2R loss-of-function state.
distractor_explanations.C: Correct. This patient has familial glucocorticoid deficiency type 1 caused by loss of the ACTH receptor MC2R. ACTH normally activates MC2R on zona fasciculata cells, coupling through Gs to adenylyl cyclase, cAMP, and protein kinase A to promote cortisol synthesis. Loss of MC2R therefore causes low cortisol despite markedly elevated ACTH. Aldosterone is classically spared because zona glomerulosa secretion is controlled mainly by the renin-angiotensin system and extracellular potassium: angiotensin II activates AT1 receptors coupled to Gq/11 and intracellular calcium signaling, and potassium depolarizes the cell membrane to increase calcium entry.
distractor_explanations.D: Incorrect. 21-hydroxylase deficiency is a steroidogenic enzyme defect that decreases cortisol and may decrease aldosterone while increasing ACTH and adrenal androgen production. It does not cause the isolated ACTH-receptor signaling defect with normal aldosterone described here.
distractor_explanations.E: Incorrect. A defect in ACTH synthesis or POMC processing would produce low or inappropriately normal ACTH rather than the marked ACTH elevation and hyperpigmentation seen with peripheral ACTH resistance.

item.lead_in: Which of the following molecular and signaling mechanisms best explains the combination of glucocorticoid deficiency and preserved mineralocorticoid secretion in this patient?

options.A: Reduced angiotensin II–AT1 receptor Gq/calcium signaling in zona glomerulosa with preserved ACTH-stimulated cAMP signaling in zona fasciculata
options.B: Failure of StAR-mediated cholesterol transfer into mitochondria throughout all steroidogenic zones of the adrenal cortex
options.C: Reduced ACTH-stimulated Gs–adenylyl cyclase–cAMP signaling in zona fasciculata with preserved angiotensin II- and potassium-dependent calcium signaling in zona glomerulosa
options.D: Loss of 21-hydroxylase activity with diversion of steroid precursors toward adrenal androgen synthesis
options.E: Failure of pituitary POMC processing with reduced ACTH secretion and intact adrenal responsiveness to ACTH

item.vignette: A 5-year-old boy is evaluated after several episodes of fasting hypoglycemia during febrile illnesses. He has diffuse hyperpigmentation of the skin and oral mucosa. Blood pressure is normal. Laboratory studies show a very low morning cortisol concentration, markedly elevated ACTH, normal serum sodium and potassium concentrations, and normal plasma renin activity and aldosterone concentration. Genetic testing identifies biallelic loss-of-function variants in MC2R.

before_BATCH_CLINICAL_Q0659_Q0683_202609.claim: Reduced angiotensin II–AT1 receptor Gq/calcium signaling in zona glomerulosa with preserved ACTH-stimulated cAMP signaling in zona fasciculata is incorrect for this vignette. Impaired angiotensin II signaling in zona glomerulosa would reduce aldosterone secretion and tend to increase renin and disturb sodium/potassium homeostasis. This patient instead has normal renin and aldosterone with isolated glucocorticoid deficiency.
before_BATCH_CLINICAL_Q0659_Q0683_202609.evidence_basis: Claim support was verified in the item-specific FINAL_10_10 clinical audit.
before_BATCH_CLINICAL_Q0659_Q0683_202609.rationale: Impaired angiotensin II signaling in zona glomerulosa would reduce aldosterone secretion and tend to increase renin and disturb sodium/potassium homeostasis. This patient instead has normal renin and aldosterone with isolated glucocorticoid deficiency.
before_BATCH_CLINICAL_Q0659_Q0683_202609.target_diagnosis_or_process: Familial glucocorticoid deficiency type 1 due to MC2R loss-of-function (ACTH resistance)
before_BATCH_CLINICAL_Q0659_Q0683_202609.target_mechanism: MC2R is the adrenal ACTH receptor and signals predominantly through Gs to adenylyl cyclase, cAMP, and protein kinase A in zona fasciculata cells to promote cortisol steroidogenesis. Loss of MC2R function therefore produces ACTH resistance with low cortisol and compensatory high ACTH. Mineralocorticoid secretion is classically preserved because aldosterone production in the zona glomerulosa is regulated primarily by angiotensin II and extracellular potassium through calcium-dependent signaling rather than by ACTH.

before_BATCH_CLINICAL_Q0659_Q0683_202609.claim: Failure of StAR-mediated cholesterol transfer into mitochondria throughout all steroidogenic zones of the adrenal cortex is incorrect for this vignette. Severe StAR dysfunction impairs the delivery of cholesterol to the inner mitochondrial membrane, compromising synthesis of multiple adrenal steroid classes rather than selectively disrupting ACTH responsiveness. It would not explain classically preserved mineralocorticoid secretion in an MC2R loss-of-function state.

before_BATCH_CLINICAL_Q0659_Q0683_202609.claim: Reduced ACTH-stimulated Gs–adenylyl cyclase–cAMP signaling in zona fasciculata with preserved angiotensin II- and potassium-dependent calcium signaling in zona glomerulosa is the uniquely best answer. This patient has familial glucocorticoid deficiency type 1 caused by loss of the ACTH receptor MC2R. ACTH normally activates MC2R on zona fasciculata cells, coupling through Gs to adenylyl cyclase, cAMP, and protein kinase A to promote cortisol synthesis. Loss of MC2R therefore causes low cortisol despite markedly elevated ACTH. Aldosterone is classically spared because zona glomerulosa secretion is controlled mainly by the renin-angiotensin system and extracellular potassium: angiotensin II activates AT1 receptors coupled to Gq/11 and intracellular calcium signaling, and potassium depolarizes the cell membrane to increase calcium entry.

blueprint.coverage_deficit_addressed: IPEX syndrome due to FOXP3 dysfunction — FOXP3 is a transcription factor required for the development and suppressive function of CD4+CD25+ regulatory T cells. Loss of FOXP3 function impairs peripheral immune tolerance, permitting widespread autoreactive lymphocyte activity and early-onset autoimmune enteropathy, endocrinopathy, and dermatitis.
blueprint.primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts

distractor_explanations.A: Incorrect. AIRE deficiency causes autoimmune polyendocrinopathy-candidiasis-ectodermal dystrophy through impaired thymic negative selection, not the FOXP3-associated regulatory-T-cell defect and classic infantile enteropathy/eczema/type 1 diabetes pattern.
distractor_explanations.B: Incorrect. CD40 ligand deficiency causes X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome with impaired class switching and susceptibility to opportunistic infections, rather than the severe early autoimmune triad of IPEX.
distractor_explanations.C: Correct. IPEX is caused by pathogenic FOXP3 variants. FOXP3 is expressed primarily in CD4+CD25+ regulatory T cells and is required for their development and suppressive function. Loss of this regulatory population permits systemic autoimmunity, classically beginning in infancy with autoimmune enteropathy, eczematous dermatitis, and endocrinopathy such as type 1 diabetes.
distractor_explanations.D: Incorrect. NADPH oxidase deficiency causes chronic granulomatous disease with defective killing of catalase-positive organisms and granuloma formation, not regulatory-T-cell failure.
distractor_explanations.E: Incorrect. Perforin-pathway defects can cause familial hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis with uncontrolled immune activation, but do not produce the characteristic FOXP3-linked loss of regulatory T-cell tolerance.

explanation.educational_objective: Connect FOXP3 loss in IPEX syndrome to defective regulatory T-cell function and failure of peripheral immune tolerance.
explanation.key_explanation: IPEX is caused by pathogenic FOXP3 variants. FOXP3 is expressed primarily in CD4+CD25+ regulatory T cells and is required for their development and suppressive function. Loss of this regulatory population permits systemic autoimmunity, classically beginning in infancy with autoimmune enteropathy, eczematous dermatitis, and endocrinopathy such as type 1 diabetes.

item.vignette: A 7-month-old boy is hospitalized for persistent watery diarrhea and poor weight gain. He has severe eczematous dermatitis and was recently diagnosed with autoimmune type 1 diabetes mellitus. His maternal uncle died in infancy after a similar illness. Genetic testing identifies a hemizygous pathogenic variant in FOXP3.

blueprint.coverage_deficit_addressed: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) — NMOSD is an autoimmune astrocytopathy strongly associated with IgG antibodies against aquaporin-4, a water channel enriched on astrocytic endfeet in the optic nerves, spinal cord, and area postrema. Attacks commonly manifest as optic neuritis, longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis, and area postrema syndrome.
blueprint.primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
blueprint.primary_system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses

distractor_explanations.A: Incorrect. Multiple sclerosis can cause optic neuritis and myelitis, but a longitudinally extensive cord lesion plus area postrema symptoms is substantially more characteristic of NMOSD.
distractor_explanations.B: Incorrect. MOG antibody-associated disease can also produce optic neuritis and longitudinally extensive myelitis, making it a strong clinical mimic; however, the detected AQP4-IgG together with area postrema symptoms identifies NMOSD rather than MOGAD.
distractor_explanations.C: Incorrect. Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis is typically a monophasic, often postinfectious syndrome with encephalopathy and multifocal CNS lesions, unlike these separated optic-spinal attacks without encephalopathy.
distractor_explanations.D: Correct. NMOSD classically affects the optic nerves and spinal cord and may involve the area postrema, causing otherwise unexplained hiccups, nausea, or vomiting. Longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis and recurrent optic neuritis are high-yield clues. Detection of AQP4-IgG makes NMOSD the uniquely best diagnosis and distinguishes it from major mimics such as MOG antibody-associated disease and multiple sclerosis.
distractor_explanations.E: Incorrect. Spinal cord infarction can cause abrupt myelopathy but does not explain a prior optic neuritis attack and area postrema syndrome.

explanation.educational_objective: Recognize NMOSD from the optic-spinal-area-postrema pattern, especially longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis.
explanation.key_explanation: NMOSD classically affects the optic nerves and spinal cord and may involve the area postrema, causing otherwise unexplained hiccups, nausea, or vomiting. Longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis, a prior attack of optic neuritis, and area-postrema symptoms are high-yield clues. Detection of AQP4-IgG makes NMOSD the uniquely best diagnosis and distinguishes it from major mimics such as MOG antibody-associated disease and multiple sclerosis.

item.vignette: A 34-year-old woman develops painful loss of vision in the right eye. Six months later, she has rapidly progressive bilateral leg weakness and urinary retention. Spinal MRI shows a T2-hyperintense lesion extending from C4 through T2. During the week before the weakness began, she had persistent hiccups and vomiting without gastrointestinal disease. Brain MRI does not show the typical periventricular lesions of multiple sclerosis. Serum testing detects IgG antibodies against aquaporin-4.

blueprint.coverage_deficit_addressed: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome — Staphylococcus aureus exfoliative toxins A and B are serine proteases that selectively cleave desmoglein-1, disrupting desmosomal adhesion in the superficial epidermis at the stratum granulosum. Desmoglein-3 is spared, helping explain mucosal sparing.
blueprint.primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts

distractor_explanations.A: Incorrect. Desmoglein-3 autoantibodies cause pemphigus vulgaris, often with prominent mucosal erosions and deeper suprabasal acantholysis.
distractor_explanations.B: Correct. SSSS is caused by toxin-producing S aureus. Exfoliative toxins A and B act as serine proteases that cleave desmoglein-1, a cadherin important for keratinocyte adhesion in the superficial epidermis. The resulting loss of adhesion causes superficial blistering, a positive Nikolsky sign, and desquamation. Mucosa is generally spared because desmoglein-3 predominates there and is not targeted by these toxins.
distractor_explanations.C: Incorrect. BP180 autoantibodies cause bullous pemphigoid with tense subepidermal bullae, generally in older adults.
distractor_explanations.D: Incorrect. Granular IgA deposition in dermal papillae is characteristic of dermatitis herpetiformis, which causes intensely pruritic grouped vesicles rather than diffuse tender superficial exfoliation.
distractor_explanations.E: Incorrect. Type VII collagen defects cause dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa with cleavage beneath the lamina densa, not toxin-mediated superficial epidermal splitting.

explanation.educational_objective: Explain SSSS as exfoliative-toxin-mediated cleavage of desmoglein-1 in the superficial epidermis.
explanation.key_explanation: SSSS is caused by toxin-producing S aureus. Exfoliative toxins A and B act as serine proteases that cleave desmoglein-1, a cadherin important for keratinocyte adhesion in the superficial epidermis. The resulting loss of adhesion causes superficial blistering, a positive Nikolsky sign, and desquamation. Mucosa is generally spared because desmoglein-3 predominates there and is not targeted by these toxins.

item.vignette: A 3-year-old boy develops fever, irritability, and diffuse skin tenderness. Over the next day, widespread erythema is followed by superficial flaccid bullae and sheet-like desquamation. Gentle pressure causes the superficial epidermis to separate. The oral mucosa is normal. A culture from the child's nasopharynx grows Staphylococcus aureus.

blueprint.coverage_deficit_addressed: Lymphangioleiomyomatosis — LAM is characterized by abnormal proliferation of smooth-muscle-like LAM cells in lung parenchyma, airways, blood vessels, and lymphatics, producing diffuse cystic lung destruction. Dysregulation of TSC1/TSC2-mTOR signaling is central, and renal angiomyolipomas are a characteristic extrapulmonary association.
blueprint.primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination

distractor_explanations.A: Incorrect. Pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis is strongly associated with cigarette smoking and typically produces irregular nodules and cysts with upper-lung predominance and relative costophrenic sparing.
distractor_explanations.B: Incorrect. Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome can cause lung cysts and pneumothorax but is associated with FLCN variants, fibrofolliculomas, and renal tumors rather than the classic LAM/angiomyolipoma pattern.
distractor_explanations.C: Incorrect. Centrilobular emphysema produces low-attenuation areas without true thin walls and is strongly related to smoking, rather than diffuse uniform cysts in a young woman with angiomyolipoma.
distractor_explanations.D: Incorrect. Lymphocytic interstitial pneumonia can cause cysts but usually occurs with autoimmune disease or immunodeficiency and commonly includes ground-glass opacities, nodules, or septal thickening.
distractor_explanations.E: Correct. A young woman with recurrent pneumothorax, diffuse bilateral thin-walled lung cysts, and a renal angiomyolipoma has lymphangioleiomyomatosis. LAM involves abnormal smooth-muscle-like cell proliferation and is linked to TSC-pathway dysregulation with mTOR activation.

explanation.educational_objective: Recognize lymphangioleiomyomatosis from diffuse thin-walled pulmonary cysts, recurrent pneumothorax, female sex, and renal angiomyolipoma.
explanation.key_explanation: A young woman with recurrent pneumothorax, diffuse bilateral thin-walled lung cysts, and a renal angiomyolipoma has lymphangioleiomyomatosis. LAM involves abnormal smooth-muscle-like cell proliferation and is linked to TSC-pathway dysregulation with mTOR activation.

item.vignette: A 32-year-old woman is evaluated after her second spontaneous pneumothorax in 18 months. She reports gradually progressive exertional dyspnea. High-resolution CT of the chest shows numerous, diffuse, round, thin-walled cysts distributed throughout both lungs with otherwise relatively preserved lung parenchyma. Abdominal imaging shows a fat-containing renal angiomyolipoma.

blueprint.coverage_deficit_addressed: Refeeding syndrome — After prolonged starvation, rapid carbohydrate delivery raises insulin. Insulin drives phosphate and potassium into cells while anabolic pathways consume phosphate for phosphorylated intermediates and ATP. Depleted total-body stores make the fall in serum phosphate particularly dangerous, causing muscle weakness, respiratory failure, arrhythmias, and neurologic dysfunction.
blueprint.primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts

distractor_explanations.A: Incorrect. PTH-mediated phosphate wasting is not the defining event after refeeding and would not explain the simultaneous characteristic insulin-linked shifts in phosphate and potassium.
distractor_explanations.B: Incorrect. Cell lysis, as in tumor lysis syndrome, releases phosphate and potassium and therefore tends to raise rather than sharply lower their serum concentrations.
distractor_explanations.C: Incorrect. Respiratory acidosis is not the mechanism of the characteristic post-refeeding electrolyte pattern; the key trigger is insulin-driven intracellular uptake after carbohydrate delivery.
distractor_explanations.D: Correct. Refeeding syndrome follows rapid nutritional replenishment after prolonged starvation. Rising glucose stimulates insulin, which drives phosphate and potassium intracellularly while anabolic metabolism increases phosphate utilization. Because total-body phosphate is already depleted, serum phosphate can fall precipitously, leading to ATP depletion, weakness, respiratory muscle dysfunction, and arrhythmias.
distractor_explanations.E: Incorrect. FGF23-mediated renal phosphate wasting can cause chronic hypophosphatemia but does not explain the abrupt multielectrolyte fall immediately after feeding a severely malnourished patient.

explanation.educational_objective: Explain refeeding syndrome as an insulin-driven intracellular shift and utilization of phosphate and other electrolytes after carbohydrate reintroduction in a severely malnourished patient.
explanation.key_explanation: Refeeding syndrome follows rapid nutritional replenishment after prolonged starvation. Rising glucose stimulates insulin, which drives phosphate and potassium intracellularly while anabolic metabolism increases phosphate utilization. Because total-body phosphate is already depleted, serum phosphate can fall precipitously, leading to ATP depletion, weakness, respiratory muscle dysfunction, and arrhythmias.

item.lead_in: Which of the following mechanisms most directly explains the new electrolyte abnormalities?

options.A: Increased parathyroid hormone secretion causes renal phosphate wasting in response to acute hypercalcemia
options.B: Cell lysis releases intracellular phosphate and potassium into the extracellular fluid after nutritional therapy begins

options.D: A carbohydrate-induced rise in insulin drives phosphate and potassium into cells during renewed anabolic metabolism

item.vignette: A 24-year-old woman with severe anorexia nervosa is admitted after several weeks of minimal food intake. On admission, she is hemodynamically stable and has a low-normal serum phosphate concentration. Enteral nutrition is started. Two days later, she develops generalized weakness, shallow breathing, and frequent ventricular ectopy. Laboratory studies show marked hypophosphatemia, hypokalemia, and hypomagnesemia.

blueprint.coverage_deficit_addressed: Typical slow-fast atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT) — Typical AVNRT requires dual AV nodal pathways: a fast pathway with rapid conduction and a relatively long refractory period, and a slow pathway with slower conduction and a shorter refractory period. A premature atrial impulse can encounter a refractory fast pathway, travel antegrade down the recovered slow pathway, then return retrograde through the now-recovered fast pathway to establish a reentrant circuit.
blueprint.primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts

distractor_explanations.A: Incorrect. Antegrade AV-nodal conduction with retrograde accessory-pathway conduction describes orthodromic AV reentrant tachycardia, not AVNRT confined to dual pathways in or adjacent to the AV node.
distractor_explanations.B: Incorrect. Macroreentry around the tricuspid annulus through the cavotricuspid isthmus is the classic mechanism of typical atrial flutter.
distractor_explanations.C: Incorrect. Focal atrial tachycardia can arise from enhanced automaticity or triggered activity, but it does not require the dual-pathway slow-fast reentry pattern and often has visible atrial activity separate from the QRS.
distractor_explanations.D: Incorrect. Catecholamine-dependent spontaneous calcium release with delayed afterdepolarizations is characteristic of catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, a ventricular rather than narrow-complex AV-nodal reentry mechanism.
distractor_explanations.E: Correct. Typical AVNRT is a slow-fast reentrant circuit using two functionally distinct AV nodal pathways. A premature atrial beat may arrive while the fast pathway is still refractory. The impulse therefore descends the slower pathway; by the time it reaches the lower common pathway, the fast pathway has recovered and can conduct retrogradely, completing the circuit. The very short RP interval and pseudo-R' in V1 are classic ECG clues.

The very short RP interval and pseudo-R' in V1 are classic ECG clues.

item.lead_in: Which of the following electrophysiologic sequences most directly initiates and sustains this arrhythmia?

options.A: The premature atrial impulse conducts antegrade through the AV node and returns retrograde to the atrium through an extranodal accessory pathway

before_BATCH_CLINICAL_Q0659_Q0683_202609.claim: The premature atrial impulse finds the fast AV nodal pathway refractory, conducts antegrade through the slow pathway, and then returns retrograde through the recovered fast pathway is the uniquely best answer. Typical AVNRT is a slow-fast reentrant circuit using two functionally distinct AV nodal pathways. A premature atrial beat may arrive while the fast pathway is still refractory. The impulse therefore descends the slower pathway; by the time it reaches the lower common pathway, the fast pathway has recovered and can conduct retrogradely, completing the circuit. The very short RP interval and pseudo-R' in V1 are classic ECG clues.

blueprint.coverage_deficit_addressed: Collagenous colitis, a subtype of microscopic colitis — Microscopic colitis produces chronic watery nonbloody diarrhea despite a grossly normal or near-normal colonoscopy. Collagenous colitis is defined histologically by a thickened subepithelial collagen band with inflammatory cells in the lamina propria; lymphocytic colitis instead has prominent intraepithelial lymphocytosis.
official_outline_path: Microscopic colitis — collagenous and lymphocytic colitis
blueprint.primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination

distractor_explanations.A: Incorrect. IBS-D can cause chronic diarrhea but does not cause the characteristic histologic thickening of the subepithelial collagen layer and usually does not produce persistent nocturnal inflammatory diarrhea.
distractor_explanations.B: Incorrect. Ulcerative colitis typically causes bloody diarrhea and visible continuous mucosal inflammation beginning in the rectum; a grossly normal colon with diagnostic microscopic collagen deposition points elsewhere.
distractor_explanations.C: Incorrect. Celiac disease causes small-intestinal villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and intraepithelial lymphocytosis rather than a thickened subepithelial collagen band in colonic biopsies.
distractor_explanations.D: Correct. Microscopic colitis should be suspected in an older adult with chronic watery nonbloody diarrhea despite a normal colonoscopic appearance. The thickened subepithelial collagen band identifies the collagenous-colitis subtype. Diagnosis requires colonic biopsies because gross mucosal appearance is often normal.
distractor_explanations.E: Incorrect. Giardiasis can cause prolonged watery or greasy diarrhea but is diagnosed by stool/duodenal testing and does not produce the defining colonic biopsy pattern.

explanation.educational_objective: Recognize collagenous microscopic colitis from chronic watery nonbloody diarrhea, normal colonoscopy, and a thickened subepithelial collagen band on biopsy.
explanation.key_explanation: Microscopic colitis should be suspected in an older adult with chronic watery nonbloody diarrhea despite a normal colonoscopic appearance. The thickened subepithelial collagen band identifies the collagenous-colitis subtype. Diagnosis requires colonic biopsies because gross mucosal appearance is often normal.

blueprint.coverage_deficit_addressed: Correct interpretation of a noninferiority trial confidence interval — In a noninferiority trial, the confidence interval for the prespecified treatment-effect contrast is compared with a clinically justified noninferiority margin. If the entire confidence interval excludes the region worse than the margin, noninferiority is demonstrated. Superiority generally requires the confidence interval also to exclude the null value in the favorable direction.
official_outline_path: Biostatistics, Epidemiology/Population Health, & Interpretation of the Medical Literature
blueprint.primary_competency: Practice-Based Learning and Improvement

distractor_explanations.A: Incorrect. A point estimate slightly favoring the control does not establish inferiority when the entire confidence interval remains above the prespecified -5-point noninferiority boundary.
distractor_explanations.B: Correct. The entire 95% confidence interval (-3.4 to +1.0) is above the prespecified noninferiority margin of -5 percentage points, so outcomes worse than the standard by 5 points or more are excluded and noninferiority is demonstrated. Because the interval crosses 0, a superiority claim is not supported. Noninferiority does not by itself prove equivalence.
distractor_explanations.C: Incorrect. Superiority would require the confidence interval to exclude the null value in the favorable direction; this interval includes zero.
distractor_explanations.D: Incorrect. Including zero prevents a superiority conclusion but does not prevent noninferiority when the entire interval remains on the acceptable side of the noninferiority margin.
distractor_explanations.E: Incorrect. A successful noninferiority test is not the same as proving exact equivalence. Equivalence requires a prespecified two-sided equivalence framework and margins.

explanation.educational_objective: Interpret a noninferiority trial by comparing the full confidence interval with the prespecified noninferiority margin and separately evaluating whether superiority is supported.

Because the interval crosses 0, a superiority claim is not supported. Noninferiority does not by itself prove equivalence.

item.difficulty_basis: Moderate author estimate: requires comparing the entire confidence interval with both the noninferiority margin and zero.
item.lead_in: Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation of these results?

options.A: The new therapy is inferior because the point estimate favors the standard therapy
options.B: The new therapy meets the prespecified criterion for noninferiority but has not demonstrated superiority to the standard therapy
options.C: The new therapy is superior because part of the confidence interval lies above zero
options.D: Noninferiority has not been demonstrated because the confidence interval includes zero
options.E: The therapies have been proven equivalent because the confidence interval lies within 5 percentage points of zero

item.vignette: A randomized trial compares a new oral therapy with an established active treatment. The primary outcome is treatment success. Before enrollment, investigators prespecify a noninferiority margin of -5 percentage points for the difference in success rates (new therapy minus standard therapy). The observed difference is -1.2 percentage points, with a 95% confidence interval of -3.4 to +1.0 percentage points.

blueprint.coverage_deficit_addressed: Post-transfusion purpura — Post-transfusion purpura is a rare alloimmune transfusion reaction in previously sensitized individuals, often multiparous women. Platelet-specific alloantibodies develop or rebound after exposure to platelet antigens in transfused blood products and cause abrupt, severe thrombocytopenia, classically several days after transfusion.
blueprint.primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination

distractor_explanations.A: Correct. Post-transfusion purpura is a delayed alloimmune transfusion reaction that classically begins about 5–12 days after transfusion and produces severe thrombocytopenia, petechiae, purpura, or bleeding. Prior pregnancies can sensitize a patient to platelet antigens. The normal coagulation tests, absence of schistocytes, lack of heparin exposure, and timing after transfusion distinguish it from DIC, TTP, and HIT.
distractor_explanations.B: Incorrect. Immune thrombocytopenia can produce isolated severe thrombocytopenia but the abrupt onset 7 days after a transfusion in a previously sensitized multiparous patient is highly characteristic of post-transfusion purpura.
distractor_explanations.C: Incorrect. TTP causes thrombocytopenia with microangiopathic hemolytic anemia and schistocytes, often with neurologic or renal findings; those features are absent.
distractor_explanations.D: Incorrect. DIC causes consumptive coagulopathy with abnormal PT/aPTT, low fibrinogen, elevated fibrin degradation markers, and often schistocytes, unlike this isolated thrombocytopenia.
distractor_explanations.E: Incorrect. HIT requires heparin exposure and usually causes a moderate platelet fall with thrombosis rather than profound isolated thrombocytopenia with bleeding; no heparin was given.

explanation.educational_objective: Recognize post-transfusion purpura as severe delayed alloimmune thrombocytopenia occurring several days after transfusion, especially in a previously sensitized multiparous patient.
explanation.key_explanation: Post-transfusion purpura is a delayed alloimmune transfusion reaction that classically begins about 5–12 days after transfusion and produces severe thrombocytopenia, petechiae, purpura, or bleeding. Prior pregnancies can sensitize a patient to platelet antigens. The normal coagulation tests, absence of schistocytes, lack of heparin exposure, and timing after transfusion distinguish it from DIC, TTP, and HIT.

item.vignette: A 61-year-old woman undergoes elective hip replacement and receives 2 units of packed red blood cells for perioperative blood loss. She has had three prior pregnancies. Seven days later, she develops diffuse petechiae and gingival bleeding. Platelet count is 7,000/mm3; it was 245,000/mm3 before surgery. Hemoglobin is stable, peripheral smear shows no schistocytes, and PT, aPTT, and fibrinogen are normal. She has not received heparin.
